title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop?
hook: Across 28,000+ tasks, agents often can't tell when to quit — some never give up when they should, others bail out only after dozens of wasted tool calls.
key_points: Agentic abstention is a multi-turn call — answer, abstain, or gather more info each step — not a one-shot answer-or-refuse decision.
Evaluated 13 LLM-as-agent systems across web shopping, terminal use, and QA on 28,000+ tasks.
Bigger or more capable models sometimes abstain worse — scale alone doesn't fix the timing problem.
Hardest failures: tasks that look feasible until the environment reveals they aren't.
CONVOLVE distills past trajectories into reusable stopping rules, lifting Llama-3.3-70B's timely-abstention recall from 26.7% to 57.4%.
content_html: Ask an agent to find a product that doesn't exist, or finish a task the environment quietly makes impossible, and plenty of them mishandle it — either grinding on forever or bailing out after burning dozens of unnecessary tool calls. A new study names this failure mode: agentic abstention, the problem of knowing when to stop acting under uncertainty.
extra_html: Unlike standard LLM abstention — a single answer-or-refuse call — agentic abstention unfolds over many turns: at each step the agent can answer, abstain, or gather more information, and the case for stopping often only becomes clear once the environment pushes back. The authors evaluate 13 LLM-as-agent systems across web shopping, terminal environments, and question answering on more than 28,000 tasks, and the core problem isn't just whether agents can abstain — it's when. Some never abstain when they should; others do it only after many wasted interactions, especially when an instruction looks feasible until the environment reveals otherwise. Model scale and reasoning don't reliably help — some larger, more capable models abstain worse. The paper's fix, CONVOLVE, distills full interaction trajectories into reusable stopping rules, more than doubling Llama-3.3-70B's timely-abstention recall on WebShop (26.7% → 57.4%) without any weight updates. Han Luo, Bingbing Wen, and Lucy Lu Wang, arXiv 2026.

related.title: ReAct: Reasoning + Acting
related.hook: Thinking alone can drift; acting alone is blind. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so an LLM can plan, look things up, and correct course — the template for agents.

related.title: Token Budgets: When Agents Burn Money
related.hook: A single retry loop can spend thousands of dollars before anyone notices. This paper catalogs 63 real budget-overrun incidents — and asks the type system to make over-spending a compile error.

related.title: Critique of Agent Model: Agentic vs. Agentive Systems
related.hook: When is a system really an 'agent' and not just a clever workflow? This paper draws the line at whether agency is internalized or scaffolded — and sketches an architecture for the former.

flashcards.prompt: Why is agentic abstention harder than a single-turn 'answer or refuse' decision?
flashcards.back_html: An agent can answer, abstain, or gather more info at every turn, and often only learns a goal is unreachable after interacting with the environment — it's a sequential judgment call, not a one-shot label.

flashcards.prompt: What did the study find about model scale and timely abstention?

choices.text: Larger or more capable models sometimes abstain worse, not better
Every model improved abstention proportionally with scale
Only small models struggled to abstain at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Scale, reasoning, and scaffolding affected abstention in inconsistent ways — larger models weren't reliably better at knowing when to stop.

flashcards.prompt: What does CONVOLVE do to improve agentic abstention?
flashcards.back_html: It distills full past interaction trajectories into reusable stopping rules — improving timely abstention without touching model weights.
